rv.q: This lavishly mounted stage adaptation of the beloved 1964. Disney film proves that sometimes more really can be more, delivering a family-friendly spectacle that should enchant children and adults alike.
Disney's Mary Poppins is a handsome, well-crafted family musical that delivers the goods without quite achieving greatness.
Her clipped diction, clasped hands and stiff poise make it clear this Mary is nobody's servant.
It's spectacular, and not even slightly boring, but anyone familiar with Walt Disney's 1964 film version of "Mary Poppins" is likely to come away asking what happened to the charm.
Even young children with great patience (is that an oxymoron?) may grow restless with the implicit lecturing between those moments when Mary flies, literally and figuratively.
Every element of the evening blends with an animated vivaciousness that lifts your spirits as easily as Mary Poppins takes off in flight, sailing to the upper balcony at the end of the evening.
Tap shoes fly vigorously in the show stopping "Step In Time" routine, highlighted by a Gavin Lee bit that is sure to be one of the most memorable moments of the season.
Mary Poppins is a show that succeeds despite itself, offering enough theatrical magic to make you believe that a spoonful of sugar really can help the medicine go down.

Forget the affable super-nanny of Disney's 1964 movie musical, Mary Poppins. As reconceived by director Richard Eyre (Iris) and codirector Matthew Bourne (the dance genius behind 1998's très gay Swan Lake), Mary (Ashley Brown) becomes a smug therapist to the cranky, morose Banks family.

cn.t: A visually lavish spectacle with dazzling effects and stagecraft, but critics find Mary Poppins emotionally distant and muddled. The production enchants with theatrical magic while struggling between saccharine sentiment and darker tones.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on center-orchestra rows D-L as the New Amsterdam's prime zone — far enough back that the Aladdin flying-carpet rig and Cave of Wonders set pieces read cleanly, but ahead of the mezzanine overhang that begins at row P. Headout specifically flags 'Center Orchestra - Any seats in Row D to K' as premium; Tickadoo calls rows D-L the spot 'where the Cave of Wonders feels truly cavernous.' Unlike most Broadway houses, the New Amsterdam 'was, by far, the most comfortable Broadway theater visited' with 'more legroom than found in other theaters,' so center orchestra here doesn't carry the usual cramped-knee penalty.

Tripadvisor's Aladdin FAQ is explicit: 'Rows A-C are too close to the stage' and 'you may miss out on a few acts that happen at the sides.' Tickadoo warns 'First few rows may require looking up' — a real cost on a show whose magic-carpet rig flies well above eyeline. The one upside is legroom: Row A gets 'extra legroom' per SeatPlan, but that is the only reason to pick front row here and the sightline penalty outweighs it for a Disney spectacle show.

The smart discount play at the New Amsterdam. Tickadoo pitches 'Rows M through Q center' as the value zone where you see 'full scope of the production's elaborate dance numbers' — key for Friend Like Me and the Genie ensemble. Headout names 'Center Orchestra - Any seats in Row F to O' as a value option. The catch that's unique to this house: 'Mezzanine Row A overhangs at Orchestra Row P,' so rows P and especially Q start losing the top of the flying rig. Aim M-O for the best value/sightline tradeoff.

Front-center mezzanine is the specific seat that Aladdin regulars recommend over center orchestra — unusual advice for a Broadway musical, but show-specific: 'The first few rows of the center Mezzanine offer perhaps the most enchanting view of Aladdin and Jasmine's magic carpet ride, where the illusion is flawless.' From the elevated vantage the wires read as invisible and the carpet 'truly appears to soar through a star-filled night sky.' RateYourSeats calls rows AA-EE 'among the best in theatre with very clear sightlines.' One caveat: 'The safety railing and lighting rig in front of row AA may cut off parts of the stage for shorter patrons' — adult seated height clears it fine but shorter kids benefit from a booster.

A quirky feature specific to this house: SeatPlan notes 'Left and Right Mezzanine rows MM-QQ are short; far aisle seats are more central than other rows.' A Tripadvisor reviewer who sat in row PP with an 8-year-old flagged the real payoff: 'THE BEST ROW IN MEZZ IS ROW MM on the side. It is a row of 4' with a private entrance, no stairs, and a group of 4 gets the whole row — no one climbing past you. Tradeoff is obvious distance and side angle, but for a family of 4 with a small child the uninterrupted private-row setup is a genuinely unusual value play.

The best of the balcony at the New Amsterdam — a distinct third tier, not a rear mezzanine. SeatPlan: 'Rows A and B of the Center Balcony still have a fair overall view' and RateYourSeats places the best balcony sightlines in 'rows A-E closest to the center of the level.' A Tripadvisor destination expert who saw Aladdin from balcony row A called the view 'excellent' and said 'the large-scale choreography was better appreciated from the balcony's elevated position' — genuinely supports the magic-carpet-from-above case. However, 'the first row of the balcony is about as far as the last row of the Orchestra Level, but from a much higher vantage point,' and row A has a safety railing that can clip the stage bottom for shorter patrons. 'Balcony seating is the least comfortable of the theater, with limited legroom.'

RateYourSeats is direct: 'Beware of rows J or higher in the side sections. In the back of the balcony are support poles that go up to the ceiling. While these are skinny and minimally invasive, they can provide a distraction and lead to partially obstructed views.' SeatPlan names specific obstructed seats from structural poles: G11, G112, H11, J10, L12. Combine thin poles, vertigo-inducing steepness ('steep angle that may be uncomfortable for patrons suffering from vertigo'), and zero legroom — ('if you purchase a balcony ticket, you will have ZERO leg room. it makes airplane seating look spacious') — and the price savings vanish.
